content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's iPhone model, which is said to be a 20th anniversary commemorative device embodying Apple's long-held vision of 'a single slab of glass.'

For a while now, reports on what we can actually expect have been all over the place, but yesterday's divergence was arguably the most stark yet…

Current situation

Apple's former design chief Jony Ive often spoke of his long-term vision of eventually turning the iPhone into a single slab of glass; even with Ive gone, it's still generally believed that Apple is moving in this direction.

While Apple doesn't generally make a big deal of anniversaries, the consensus in the industry is that they're targeting achieving this vision as close to the iPhone 20th anniversary as possible. This is very likely to include embedding Face ID under the screen, as well as hiding the front camera beneath the display.

However, we've already seen conflicting reports on these expectations. The original view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports say the design will appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In sequence, that would be the iPhone 19 Pro, although Apple could also choose to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday's situation was muddied further by an analyst claiming that Apple had abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone for next year.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, however, promptly pushed back on this claim.

The more likely reality

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single endpoint. What they plan to deliver next year is just one step, or a few steps, toward the sci-fi vision of 'a single slab of glass.'

The question isn't whether this goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move toward it. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in the evolution of the iPhone's design.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has actually pulled back somewhat from the goals originally expected for next year.

The Jefferies analyst likely received the same information, but a beat late and mistook it for the entire plan being shelved.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap forward — comparable to the breakthrough of the iPhone X — but with more development to come in the years after. For me, the big question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have a big enough breakthrough to be worth marking with some kind of special branding, such as labeling it a 20th anniversary iPhone edition (which I consider highly unlikely), giving it another special name, or skipping a generation and calling it the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Share them in the comments.
